---
title: "Reviewing deviation and CAPA write-ups"
order: 30
---

## The ticket

Your Quality Analyst (QA) routes you a deviation and CAPA (corrective and preventive action)
packet for supervisory review: the ICCBBA (International Council for Commonality in Blood
Banking Automation, the organization that governs the barcode standard on every unit Lakeshore
ships) product-code-table event from the processing lab — the one where a vendor update to BECS
(Blood Establishment Computer Software, the system that gates donor eligibility, quarantine
release, and label printing) pushed mid-shift, and roughly 40 units printed final labels against
a table that had just gone stale underneath them. It never got written up as a deviation at the
time. Now it has, and it's sitting in your queue with a note: "Ready to close. Need your
sign-off."

You already know exactly which box you're being asked to sign, because the last module made you
work it out the hard way: this is supervisory review, squarely yours. Not the quality decision —
disposition and reportability belong to whoever Lakeshore's SOP names for that, and it isn't you.
Your question is narrower and, this time, entirely within your authority: is this document
defensible? Would it survive someone reading it cold, a year from now, with her not in the room?

## Why this matters — and the ITIL bridge

You already review this shape of document every week, just under a different name: a direct
report's postmortem or post-incident review (PIR). You check for contributing factors, action
items with named owners, and whether those action items actually closed instead of quietly
aging out. None of that instinct is wrong here. What's new is how much further the quality
version has to go before it's actually finished.

A postmortem's worst common failure is "third-party outage, no action" — the vendor's platform
went down, so the story ends there, and nobody asks what Lakeshore's own monitoring, failover, or
contract terms should have caught first. You're about to read a write-up with exactly that shape,
wearing a different vendor's name. Where this version demands more than any postmortem you've
reviewed: a reportability call that starts a legal clock at discovery, not at write-up; a
disposition decision that has to sit with a specific, SOP-named authority, not whoever's closest
to the keyboard; an effectiveness check that has to be able to fail; and a reader — an FDA
investigator or AABB assessor — who can cite Lakeshore a finding for missing reasoning even when
the conclusion turns out to have been right. "I'd have approved this ticket" and "this would
survive an inspector" are different bars, and this module is where you learn to read for the
second one on a real, complete document.

## The rule in plain English — how to actually review one of these

Don't read a deviation and CAPA packet front to back. Read it in the order an assessor reads it,
because that order is what actually tests the document:

1. **Start with the conclusions.** What's the disposition? What's the reportability call? Read
   these first and hold them loosely — you're about to check whether anything on the rest of the
   page actually earns them.
2. **Then the evidence and extent.** What's the proof behind each conclusion, and does it cover
   the *whole* claim — every affected unit, the *whole* time window, not just the part someone
   happened to notice?
3. **Then the root cause.** Is it systemic, or does it stop at the first plausible-sounding
   external explanation?
4. **Then the effectiveness check**, last, because it only means anything once you know what it's
   supposed to be checking.

That's a deliberate reversal of how the document is written — narrative first, checks last.
Reading conclusions first, before the narrative primes you, keeps you from unconsciously grading
the document on how convincing the story sounds instead of on whether it's actually proven.

Once you've read it that way, run the same instrument module 1 gave you — the **cold-read test**
— named exactly the same six ways every time: **Conclusion, Evidence, Reasoning, Criteria first,
Decision trail, Loose ends.** Sort whatever it finds with **gap triage**: **must fix before I
sign**, **fix going forward**, or **fine as is**. Neither instrument gets re-taught here — you
already have them. This is the first time you point them at a real, complete document instead of
a one-line example.

Three things make this review harder than a postmortem, worth naming before you read the packet:

**The Director-only IT-evidence check.** Somewhere in almost every document your QA writes,
there's a claim IT evidence could confirm or break, and you're often the only reviewer positioned
to know that evidence exists and where it lives — a BECS change or deployment log, print-job
history, a table-version timestamp, a deployment date next to an approval signature. A Quality
reviewer without your background can only take the write-up's word for these. You can go check.

**"Polished but hollow."** A well-formatted document, with clean headings and every field filled
in, can be *less* defensible than a terse one — the formatting itself signals confidence the
content hasn't earned. Don't let good formatting lower your guard; read a document that looks this
clean more slowly, not less.

**Consistency across documents.** Does the CAPA's stated cause actually match the facts the
deviation record already established? A CAPA that quietly narrows what the deviation found is its
own kind of gap, even when each document reads fine alone.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 606.100(b)(16) | "Six-oh-six point one-hundred, paragraph b, sub-sixteen" | Written SOPs must cover "labeling procedures, including safeguards to avoid labeling mixups." | The exact safeguard that failed: a vendor content push reached the label printers mid-shift with nothing stopping labels from printing against a table that had just changed underneath them. |
| 21 CFR 606.100(c) | "...paragraph c" | Records reviewed before release; a thorough investigation, "including the conclusions and followup," of any discrepancy. | Already the backbone of the deviation and CAPA modules in `quality-system-essentials` — the word "conclusions" is exactly what this packet's reportability line is missing. |
| 21 CFR 606.171(b)(1)(i) / (b)(3) | "...paragraph b, sub-one, clause i / sub-three" | A deviation from CGMP or an applicable regulation, that may affect safety, purity, or potency, *and* involves distributed product, is reportable. | The actual test behind "Not reportable." The second prong — distribution — is met only if nothing shipped, which is exactly the fact this packet never proves. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(7)(iii) | "...paragraph b, sub-seven, clause iii" | Biological product deviations are kept among an establishment's general records. | The record requirement this whole packet exists to satisfy — reused from module 1. |

## The actual text

The labeling-safeguards requirement, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md` — not quoted by
any earlier lesson in this curriculum:

> (16) Labeling procedures, including safeguards to avoid labeling mixups.

The regulatory floor underneath the whole event: a vendor's content push landing on the print
floor mid-shift, with nothing routed for Quality's review, is exactly the kind of gap this clause
exists to prevent — a safeguard that either wasn't there or didn't fire.

The investigation standard, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.100.md`, already the backbone of
two `quality-system-essentials` modules:

> All records pertinent to the lot or unit maintained pursuant to these regulations shall be
> reviewed before the release or distribution of a lot or unit of final product... A thorough
> investigation, including the conclusions and followup, of any unexplained discrepancy or the
> failure of a lot or unit to meet any of its specifications shall be made and recorded.

Hold onto "including the conclusions." A reportability line that states an answer with no visible
reasoning hasn't produced a conclusion in this clause's sense — it's produced an assertion.

The reportability test itself, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.171.md`:

> (b) ... You must report any event... if that event meets all the following criteria: (1)(i)
> Represents a deviation from current good manufacturing practice, applicable regulations,
> applicable standards, or established specifications that may affect the safety, purity, or
> potency of that product; or... and (3) Involves distributed blood or blood components.

Two prongs, both required. The first isn't really in dispute here; printing against a stale
ICCBBA table is exactly the kind of deviation this clause has in mind. The second — "involves
distributed blood or blood components" — is where this document actually lives or dies: if
nothing shipped, "not reportable" is right; if something did, the call flips. The whole
determination rests on one unproven fact.

And the record requirement, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`, reused from module 1:

> (7) General records: ... (iii) Biological product deviations.

## The packet on your desk

Here it is, formatted and routed the way your QA actually sends these — competent at first
glance, headings filled in, signatures in place:

> **LAKESHORE BLOOD CENTER — DEVIATION REPORT AND CAPA SUMMARY**
>
> **Deviation ID:** DEV-1147 &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Status:** Closed &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Date opened:**
> Wed 09/03 &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Date closed:** 09/10
> **CAPA ID:** CAPA-1147-A &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Status:** Open &nbsp;|&nbsp; **Date opened:** 09/05
> **Prepared by:** Quality Analyst
>
> **Description:** BECS deployment log shows the vendor's quarterly ICCBBA product code table
> update applied at 01:58 a.m. Wednesday, outside any scheduled change window and without prior
> routing to Quality.
>
> **Extent of condition:** Approximately 40 units affected — predominantly leukoreduced red
> blood cells, plus several pooled cryoprecipitate units — printed final labels between 02:00
> and 06:15 a.m. against the prior table version.
>
> **Investigation:** Third-shift Processing Supervisor M. Colvin noticed a product code
> mismatch at 06:15 a.m. shift change and halted printing. Per Supervisor Colvin, none of the
> affected units have shipped; all remain in Lakeshore inventory pending relabel.
>
> **Root cause:** The BECS vendor pushed the ICCBBA table update without notifying Lakeshore in
> advance.
>
> **Reportability determination (21 CFR 606.171):** Not reportable.
>
> **Disposition:** Relabel all affected units against the current ICCBBA table and release to
> inventory.
> *Signed:* M. Colvin, Processing Supervisor. **Date:** 09/03.
> *Reviewed:* Quality Analyst. **Date:** 09/05.
>
> ---
>
> **CAPA-1147-A**
>
> **Corrective action:** All 40 affected units relabeled and re-verified against the current
> ICCBBA table; completed 09/04.
>
> **Preventive actions:**
> 1. Reassess the BECS vendor, focused on change notification.
> 2. Pursue a contract amendment requiring advance notice of future ICCBBA table pushes.
>    Target date: TBD.
>
> **Effectiveness check:** Vendor has confirmed it will notify Lakeshore in advance of future
> ICCBBA table updates.
>
> **Prepared by:** Quality Analyst. **Date:** 09/05.

**Before you read on: run the cold-read test yourself. Find the gaps, and decide what you'd send
back — you have everything you need.**

## The reveal

Organized by the six questions, not by the document's own order — because that's how you'd
actually work it, and because the document's order is part of what's hiding the gaps.

**Conclusion.** Clean, actually. There are exactly two, each stated plainly: disposition
(relabel and release) and reportability (not reportable). No gap here — worth noting explicitly,
because not every finding on a real document is a problem, and pretending otherwise trains
defensive writing.

**Evidence.** This is where the packet actually breaks, in two connected ways.

First: "none of the affected units have shipped" rests entirely on Supervisor Colvin's word. Not
an unreasonable person to ask — he's who caught it — but his statement isn't evidence that
nothing shipped, it's a starting point for finding evidence. `component-processing-and-labeling`
already named the artifact an inspector would ask for: a BECS distribution or inventory query, run
against all 40 affected donation identification numbers (DINs), showing where every one of them
is right now. That query isn't in this document, and nothing suggests it was run. This is your
QA's pattern in its most common shape: stopping at the first credible-sounding source instead of
the source that actually proves the claim. A supervisor's say-so is credible. It isn't proof.

Second — one you're positioned to catch in a way Quality alone often isn't: the investigation is
scoped to 02:00–06:15 a.m., the window Supervisor Colvin happened to be watching. That's not the
same thing as the actual exposure window. The deployment log already in this document puts the
push at 01:58 a.m. — so where's the record showing printing was fully corrected right after 06:15,
and not still running against the stale table for another ten minutes at a second print station
nobody was watching? You know where that record lives: the table-version-change history and
print-job log BECS keeps, tied to the same DINs. A reviewer without your background would have no
reason to ask for it — they'd read "02:00 to 06:15" as a fact about the world instead of a fact
about when one person happened to be looking. That gap is genuinely yours to catch.

Triage: **must fix before I sign.** Both threads feed directly into the reportability call below —
this isn't a cosmetic gap, it's the one everything else is standing on.

**Reasoning.** Two separate issues, both instances of the same underlying pattern.

The reportability line — "not reportable" — states a conclusion with no reasoning shown at all.
Run the actual test from 606.171(b): the first prong (a deviation that may affect safety, purity,
or potency) is close to undeniable here. The second prong — distribution — is where the real
argument has to live, and it's exactly the fact the Evidence section just showed is unproven. The
conclusion is very likely correct. The write-up just doesn't show its work, which means right now
it's an assertion wearing a conclusion's clothes. Triage: on its own, this would be **fix going
forward** — add the reasoning, the conclusion probably survives. Combined with the unproven
evidence underneath it, though, it's part of the same **must fix before I sign** finding above.
This is the other half of your QA's pattern: usually right, reasoning off the page.

The root cause — "the vendor pushed the update without notifying Lakeshore" — is a different kind
of reasoning problem: not thin, but pointed at the wrong system. It's vendor-blame, the external
twin of "human error," and the exact "third-party outage, no action" shape a bad postmortem takes.
`becs-in-the-pipeline` already named the real cause when this event first surfaced: not that the
vendor is untrustworthy, but that Lakeshore's own change model treats a vendor's content push to
BECS as a data refresh instead of a change — nothing in Lakeshore's process routed it for review
before it hit the print floor. Notice what the wrong root cause does downstream: every preventive
action in this CAPA is aimed at the vendor (reassess them, amend their contract), and none touch
Lakeshore's own change classification. A misdiagnosed root cause visibly steers the fix. Triage:
**must fix before I sign.**

**Criteria first.** The effectiveness check — "vendor has confirmed it will notify Lakeshore in
advance of future ICCBBA table updates" — is a promise, not a check. Run the test
`capa-root-cause-to-effectiveness` already gave you: could this fail? No. It only records that the
vendor said something; it doesn't measure whether the failure mode actually stopped, and it has no
data source, no time window, and no pre-agreed definition of what "not effective" would even look
like. It's implementation evidence dressed up as a result. Triage: **must fix before I sign** — as
written, this CAPA cannot close on a real effectiveness result, because none is possible from what
it says.

**Decision trail.** The disposition — relabel and release — is signed by M. Colvin, Processing
Supervisor, on 09/03. Lakeshore's SOP consistently names "the medical director or a delegated
quality officer" as disposition authority — the same authority module 1's stack almost let you
sign over by mistake. It isn't the processing supervisor's box, however well-formatted the
signature line looks. Notice the date too: the disposition is signed 09/03, two days *before* the
Quality Analyst's own review on 09/05 — the units were already released before anyone with a
documented review role had looked at the file. Triage: **must fix before I sign.** A structural
authority gap, not a stylistic one — the kind of thing an assessor finds in the time it takes to
read two signature lines.

**Loose ends.** Two things live here, and they're not the same kind of finding.

First, notice what's *not* wrong: the deviation record is closed while the CAPA is still open.
That's exactly right — `deviations-and-nonconformances` already taught you these run on different
clocks. Closing the deviation says "we know what happened to the product and made the required
calls." Closing the CAPA, separately and later, says "we've proven the system won't do this
again." If you flagged this as an inconsistency, that's a fair instinct to have and a useful
correction to get now, on a document where it costs nothing — the two statuses being different
isn't the gap.

The real loose end sits inside the still-open CAPA: preventive action 2, "pursue a contract
amendment... target date: TBD," has no owner and no date — exactly what this question is built to
catch. Triage: **fix going forward.** It doesn't undermine anything the packet has concluded so
far, but it can't stay TBD forever on a document someone will eventually check for aging.

**One line before you move on.** If "none shipped" turns out to be wrong once someone actually
runs the BECS query, the reportability picture changes — a distributed unit would flip prong two
of 606.171(b) — and that's the kind of thing that would need to reach you fast, not wait for the
next scheduled review. Deciding how fast, and through what path, is `escalation-criteria`'s job;
this module only teaches you to notice when a review has surfaced that kind of trigger.

**Sending it back.** The move isn't to rewrite the document yourself — that trains your QA to wait
for your red pen instead of writing more carefully the first time. Send it back with questions:

- "What BECS record shows none of the 40 units shipped — can you run the distribution query
  against all 40 DINs and attach it?"
- "What does the table-version-change and print-job history show, start to finish — not just
  the window Supervisor Colvin was watching?"
- "Walk me through the reasoning behind 'not reportable' — what does it depend on?"
- "If a different vendor pushed something similar next quarter, what in our own process would
  catch it before it reached the print floor?"
- "What would tell us the vendor's promise is working, six months from now, that isn't just
  their word again?"
- "Who signs disposition on this per our SOP, and has that person actually reviewed it?"
- "Who owns the contract-amendment action, and by when?"

## What an inspector or assessor would actually look for

An assessor pulling this same file runs a version of the review you just did, without you in the
room to ask follow-ups — which is exactly why the answers have to already be in writing. They'll
ask for the BECS distribution query against all 40 DINs, not the supervisor's statement. They'll
pull the table-version-change and print-job logs themselves and check them against the stated
02:00–06:15 window, because that's a record they know how to request. They'll read the
effectiveness check and ask, in some form, "how would this fail?" — a check that can't gets
written up on its own. And they'll check the disposition signature against Lakeshore's own SOP,
because a mismatch there isn't a technicality — it's evidence the quality system doesn't actually
control who decides what. A bad answer to "how do you know nothing shipped" sounds exactly like
this document reads: "the supervisor said so." A good answer is a query result with a timestamp.

## Common traps

**"A supervisor's word is good enough — he's the one who caught it."** He's a credible source for
what he personally observed, not a substitute for a system-of-record query — and the difference
matters most exactly when a regulatory conclusion depends on it, the way "not reportable" depends
here on "none shipped."

**"The conclusion is probably right, so the missing reasoning doesn't matter."** The trap built
for a document like this one. "Not reportable" is likely correct — that doesn't make the write-up
defensible. An assessor doesn't grade on whether you landed on the right answer; they grade on
whether the page shows how you got there. A right answer with no shown reasoning is still a
finding.

**Vendor-blame as root cause.** "The vendor didn't notify us" feels like an explanation because it
names a real fact. It isn't a root cause unless nothing on Lakeshore's side could plausibly have
caught it — and here, something could have: Quality review of BECS changes, which this event never
got routed through. Blaming the vendor is the deviation-and-CAPA world's "third-party outage, no
action," and it produces the same downstream failure: preventive actions aimed entirely outward,
while the internal gap stays open.

## What this means for your job

- **Read conclusions first, evidence and extent second, root cause third, effectiveness check
  last.** Reading front to back lets the narrative sell you the ending before you've checked
  whether it's earned.
- **Whenever a document says "none," "nothing," or "no impact," ask what query or record proves
  it — not who said it.** A named, credible source is a lead, not evidence.
- **Distrust any effectiveness check phrased as a promise, a confirmation, or "the vendor says."**
  If you can't picture what a *failed* version of that check would look like, it isn't one.
- **Know where your own IT evidence lives, and go get it yourself when a claim depends on it** —
  deployment logs, print-job history, table-version timestamps, a deployment date next to an
  approval signature. This is the one check in the whole packet nobody but you is positioned to
  run.
- **Send gaps back as questions, sorted by gap triage, not as a rewritten document.** A "must fix
  before I sign" question demands an answer before you sign anything. A "fix going forward" note
  can wait for the next draft without holding up this one.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: A different CAPA closes with: "Effectiveness check: BECS help desk confirms the corrected downtime binder was mailed to all satellite sites." Real effectiveness check, or something else?

Implementation evidence, not an effectiveness check — the same gap as this module's vendor
promise, wearing a different vendor. It confirms an action happened; it doesn't check whether the
failure mode actually stopped, because of course the binders were mailed once the corrective
action was done. Ask instead: what data source, checked on what schedule, could show a site was
still running a superseded binder, and what result would count as a fail? Confirming the mailing
is worth recording — it just isn't the check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: A different deviation states, "Root cause: donor phlebotomy station was short-staffed that shift, so the pre-donation history review was rushed." Is naming a staffing shortage as root cause a "must fix before I sign," "fix going forward," or "fine as is"?

Must fix before I sign — vendor-blame's sibling, not a real root cause. "Short-staffed" describes
a condition, not a system failure: it doesn't explain why the process has no control that catches
a rushed review when staffing is thin. Run the same test used on the vendor: if the exact same
shift happened again, same staffing level, would anything go differently? As written, no. Push one
level further before it's a real root cause.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: A vendor risk questionnaire states, "Vendor confirms it maintains 24/7 monitoring of its platform," and the QA's write-up treats that as evidence the monitoring requirement is met. What's the parallel to this module's evidence gap?

The same "stops at the first credible source" pattern, one document type over. A vendor's own
self-attestation is a credible-sounding source — it's still the vendor's word about itself, not
independent proof. The question is the same one you'd ask about "none shipped": what's the
evidence *behind* the claim — an audit result, a report, a log excerpt — not just the claim
restated with a vendor's name attached to it. You'll see this shape again when this course reaches
vendor risk assessments.
:::

## Where this goes next

This module was about a document: something written after the fact, judged on whether it would
survive a cold read. The next module, `escalation-criteria`, is about an event: something
happening in real time, often before any document exists at all, judged on whether it reaches you
— and how fast. A review like the one you just ran can surface an escalation trigger a document's
author missed entirely, the way an unproven "none shipped" claim did here. Recognizing that moment
is as far as this module goes; sorting it into "call me now" versus "tell me at our one-on-one" is
next.
